content: This medication should only be used during pregnancy if it is clearly necessary. It may be part of a treatment plan to reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to your baby. However, it is not known whether this medication passes into breast milk. Drug interactions can alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. It is important to maintain a list of all the products you use, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and herbal supplements, and share this list with your doctor and pharmacist. Some products, such as orlistat, may interact with this medication. If someone overdoses and experiences severe symptoms like loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Before starting this medication and while taking it, laboratory and medical tests (such as liver function tests, viral load, and T-cell counts) should be conducted. It is essential to keep all medical and laboratory appointments. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is close to the time of your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Do not double the dose to catch up. Store this medication at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs. Common side effects may include cough, stomach pain, tiredness, lightheadedness, or dizziness, especially when standing. If your immune system becomes stronger, it may begin to fight off infections you already had, potentially causing symptoms of those infections to reappear. In some cases, an overactive immune response may occur. This reaction can happen at any time, either shortly after starting HIV treatment or months later. A severe allergic reaction to this drug is rare. However, this is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Before taking this medication, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems. This drug may cause dizziness. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate this effect. Avoid driving, using machinery, or performing tasks that require alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. It may be part of a treatment plan to reduce the risk of transmitting HIV to your baby. It is unknown if this medication passes into breast milk. Always consult your healthcare provider for guidance.
